PREVENTIVE DENTISTRY FLUORIDE PROGRAM STANDARD The Board of Health shall ensure: (1) (a) That the fluoride level in the water supply of those communities where fluoride is added to the water, be monitored at least once per month. (b) That where the results of such monitoring indicate a fluoride level other than 1.2 ppm, the persons responsible for the operation of the water supply are notified of such results in order that action can be taken to bring the fluoride level to 1.2 ppm. (2) That water ‘luoridation be promoted in communities where the natural fluoride level is below 0.7 ppm. (3) That a program of fluoride supplements be promoted for children up to the age of 13 with particular emphasis on preschool children in communities where the level of fluoride in water system(s) is below 0.7 ppm. IMPLEMENTATION (1) Program Monitoring In order to indicate whether or not the Standard has been complied with, the following minimum information shall be provided, on request, to the Ministry of Health: (a) Details of the monitoring programs carried out under item (1a) of the Standard and the results thereof. (b) Evidence, satisfactory to the Ministry, that promotional campaigns as envisaged under items (2) and (3) of the Standard have been conducted. (2) Staffing The services and activities referred to in the Standard shall be carried out by public health dental staff under the direction of the Board of Health’s senior ranking public health dentist, with other staff being assigned where appropriate. (3) Program Delivery (a) The intent of item (2) of the Standard may be met through: (i) promotion of water fluoridation through such measures as the media, displays, presentations to community groups. (ii) the testing of water in non-fluoridated areas on request. (b) Under item (3) of the Standard the Fluoride
Standard may be met through: (i) promotion of water fluoridation through such measures as the media, displays, presentations to community groups. (ii) the testing of water in non-fluoridated areas on request. (b) Under item (3) of the Standard the Fluoride Supplement Program shall be carried out in accordance with accepted standards of practise. (c) The use of supplements shall be promoted in non-fluoridated areas for infants and children up to age 13 through the family physicians, dentists and other community health professionals.

Additional statistical data on the delivery of the Chil- dren’s Dental Program by the Manitoba Dental Associ- ation is contained ir the Statistical Appendix. Acomprehensive preventive dental program in schools is directed to students from Kindergarten to Grade 8. Students in the primary grades (Kindergarten to Grade 3) participated in the daily brushing program at a great- er frequency than students at the higher grade levels. Dental health education programs above the Grade 8 level are provided on a request basis. Schools are en- couraged to participate in the weekly fluoride rinse pro- gram to include all Kindergarten to Grade 12 students. A kindergarten preventive dental program was offered to Kindergarten children enrolled in school based, den- tal nurse delivery areas. Children received a dental screening, cleaning, fluoride treatment and oral hygiene instruction. Parents received notification of their child’s dental health status, and their future eligi- bility in the treatment program. The preventive programs are offered to all school divi- sions outside the City of Winnipeg. There are current- ly 69,705 children eligible for preventive dental programs: classroom education, weekly fluoride rinse or daily brushing sessions offered by Dental Health. Dental Health provides public health/preventive pro- grams to senior citizen centres, to centres for the men- tally handicapped and to child day care centres. Dental treatment services are provided to patients at Brandon Mental Health Centre. Dental staff also provide consul- tant functions for the department of Family Services, Social Allowances Dental Health Services section. Educational and consultation services are provided on request to prenatal and postnatal classes, career days in schools, parent meetings, preschoolers, information- al seminars, teacher inservices and other health profes- sionals. Staff are also actively involved in educational activities in conjunction with Dental Health Month. During this fiscal year, Dental Health provided funding for special grants
in schools, parent meetings, preschoolers, information- al seminars, teacher inservices and other health profes- sionals. The branch also continued to oper- ate the water fluoridation program in 73 communities representing 95% of the population on a public water supply. This program involves providing technical as- sistance to communities to maintain the correct level of fluoride in the water supply. In addition, funding is provided to communities to purchase fluoridation equipment. Wabowden, Sanford and Gilbert Plains received funding to begin fluoridating in 1989/90. instance. For the longer term, we see no reason why healthcare regionalization necessarily requires a different approach. Conventional labour relations wisdom favours fewer, rather than more, bargaining units. That conventional wisdom is consistent with what has been the approach of this Board all along. The next word from the Board was the case of Canadian Health Care Guild and Alberta Union of Provincial Employees v. Peace Regional Health Authority et al. [1996] Alta. L.R.B.R. 106, another certification case, this time involving competing applications for units of community health support employees. The Board after a detailed review of the appropriateness factors at play in that application, reached the same result as in Regional Health Authority 5 -- the site- specific units were deemed inappropriate and AUPE's region-wide application was allowed to proceed. Two points leap out from the Board's analysis in the case: First, community health units in a regional structure would not necessarily follow precedents allowing site-specific units in hospitals. Second, the bargaining history in community health militates against site-specific units. The former Peace River Health Unit, the largest health unit absorbed into the new regional authority, had like other health units in Alberta, bargained on a unit-wide basis. By applying for units based on individual area offices, the Guild had applied for units smaller than existed before regionalization. This attracted the Board's historic opposition to fragmenting existing bargaining structures and the applications failed even though several other factors pointed to the site- specific units being at least somewhat appropriate. The Peace Regional Health Authority case highlights one important difference between hospital and community health bargaining units: while many hospitals have been certified on a site basis -- or as part of a hospital district in which it was the only acute care facility -- health units have almost always
between hospital and community health bargaining units: while many hospitals have been certified on a site basis -- or as part of a hospital district in which it was the only acute care facility -- health units have almost always bargained on an employer-wide basis. Going to site-based bargaining units in community health after regionalization therefore amounts to fragmentation of existing bargaining structures; recognizing site-based hospital units often does not. If, as Peace Regional Health Authority suggests, the policy against fragmentation dictates that the Board not allow site-specific units in community health after regionalization, what other alternatives are there? Presumably one choice is between a region-wide community health unit and units based on the old health unit boundaries. But what organizational basis could exist for units based on the old health unit boundaries? pages.text:
Alberta Labour Relations Board Discussion Paper — Standard Health Care Bargaining Units 01/24/02 32 One remaining question is how to implement this new bargaining unit structure and yet respect the rights of those paramedical professionals or technical employees who remain unorganized. Consistent with the previous recommendations, the parties should first attempt to reach their own resolution. RECOMMENDATION #20 The Board initiate a review of all current paramedical professional and paramedical technical units and encourage the parties to negotiate a process to merge all paramedical professional and technical certificates for the same employer within a health region by December 31, 2003. If the parties are unable to negotiate and implement a resolution, the Board take steps to bring the certificates within the policy of combining paramedical professional and technical certificates of the same employer within the same health region or within the governance model of the employer. Where consolidated certificates would sweep in currently non-union sites or groups, the Board: identify those non-union sites or groups as exceptions to the employer-wide certificate, conduct a vote of the non-union group to determine their wishes, or include the non-union group in the certificate by agreement of the parties and employees. B. Community Health The Board currently uses three standard functional units in community health. Those units are: 1. all employees when employed in community health nursing. 2. all employees when employed in a community health professional or technical capacity. 3. all employees when employed in a community health support capacity . Those units have continued to function well for the Board and the parties In Information Bulletin T-2, the Board signaled that, if the acute care sector and the community health sector integrated, it would combine the sectors and the bargaining units, but in doing so would divide the three community health units
parties In Information Bulletin T-2, the Board signaled that, if the acute care sector and the community health sector integrated, it would combine the sectors and the bargaining units, but in doing so would divide the three community health units into the five acute care standard units. The Board could either continue with these standard functional units or move now to restructure the community health units to match the four standard functional units used elsewhere in the industry. A change now would require splitting the community health support unit into two parts — auxiliary nursing care and general support services. Those units would become region-wide community health units. They would be flexible enough to allow the Board to later (as the industry develops) merge the community health and facilities units without much disruption.

adjudication.reason: Read both pages. Page A's sentence continues 'health units have almost always bargained on an employer-wide basis', so claim A is on the page; page B lists three community health units. Different questions about bargaining units: not comparable is the honest answer. The judge's complaint about 'a1'/'b1' is about quote ids, which visitors never see.

claude-haiku-5-5.notes: The explanation and both claims are supported by the pages: Page A says health units bargained employer-wide while many hospitals were site-certified, and Page B lists three standard community health units and a restructuring option. Calling the pages not comparable is a defensible answer, since they address different questions about bargaining units. The round is not fair or clear to a visitor, though. The claim quote fields contain placeholders ('a1', 'b1') and the decisive list holds placeholder IDs ('d1', 'd2', 'd3'), so they would appear as meaningless text. A person should fix these fields before display.

verdicts.notes: All quotes appear verbatim on the cited pages; claim A's quote is truncated just before 'bargained on an employer-wide basis' but the page continues with exactly that wording. Page A concerns site-based versus employer-wide units and past bargaining history, while Page B concerns the number of functional unit types (three vs four) in community health, so 'not comparable' is the honest call; the French matches the English.

explanation.en: Both pages are payment lists from the British Columbia Medical Services Plan, for different years. The rule for which accounts are listed one by one is not the same: one lists each account of $500 or more, the other each account of more than $10,000. Because the lists count different sets of payments, they cannot be set side by side as a change in the same thing or as a disagreement. What changed is the listing rule, not a figure the two pages share.
explanation.fr: Les deux pages sont des listes de paiements du Medical Services Plan de la Colombie-Britannique, pour des années différentes. La règle qui décide quels comptes sont listés un par un n'est pas la même : l'une liste chaque compte de 500 $ ou plus, l'autre chaque compte de plus de 10 000 $. Comme les listes comptent des ensembles de paiements différents, on ne peut y voir ni un changement de la même chose ni un désaccord. Ce qui a changé, c'est la règle de la liste, pas un chiffre commun aux deux pages.

Present Status of Children's Dental Health Essentially all children 12 years of age and younger are receiving regular dental care and have good dental health. As a result of the program cutback in April 1983 many children aged 13-16 years are not receiving any dentai treatment or preventive services, and will develop serious dental problems in the near future. Most children aged 13-16 years still have relatively good dental health as a maximum of only two years has elapsed since they were removed from the children’s program. Re- ports from dentists throughout the province suggest that approximately 50% of teenaged children in rural areas and 40% of teenaged children in urban areas are not receiving reg- ular dental treatment. To date there are few reports of teeth being extracted as a result of lack of treatment. However, there is little doubt that the majority of children not receiving regular dental care will accumulate carious teeth and will eventually require the extraction of teeth. The Preventive Orthodontic Program provides preventive and interceptive ortho- dontic services to children covered under the Children’s Dental Care Program. The objec- tives of the program are to provide good function and acceptable appearance using sim- ple methods, thereby eliminating the need for complex orthodontic treatment at a later date. This program provides services to approximately one-third of all children at one time or another. Each year 700-800 children are referred to the clinic by private dentists and Clinic dentists. Dental Manpower The province has an adequate supply of dentists who are well distributed throughout the province. There is also an adequate supply of dental hygienists and dental assistants in all areas of the province. Present indications are that a surplus of dentists will develop over the next few years. Demonstration Project A demonstration project to assess the long term effectiveness of fissure sealants in preventing dental caries has been in operation for the past six years. Fissure sealants are plastic films which are used to cover the fissures and groves of the biting surfaces of teeth and thereby prevent dental caries on these tooth surfaces. After five years 82% of all sealed tooth surfaces remained successfully sealed. An ad- ditional 12% of sealed teeth were restored due to dental caries on non-sealed surfaces. Only 3% of sealed surfaces required restorations due to failure of the sealant. Fissure sealants are now being provided routinely in Department Clinics with very im- pressive results. DIVISION OF DENTAL PUBLIC HEALTH Dr. R.G. Romcke, Director The purpose of the Dental Division is to assist Prince Edward Islanders to achieve and maintain good dental health. Major activities include the Children’s Dental Care Program, the Preventive Orthodontic Program and a Geriatric Dental Program. The Division’s administration office and the Preventive Orthodontic Clinic are located in the Sullivan Building, while four large mobile dental clinics operate in various centres throughout the province. Dental clinics are also operated at the Summerside Health Centre and the St. Jeans Elementary School in Charlottetown. In addition, Preventive Dental Clinics are operated on a part-time basis in Tignish, O’ Leary, Crapaud, Abrams Village, Morell, Souris, Montague and Murray River. Further improvements in the dental health of children were achieved during the past year with lower average treatment needs, and with more children having dental caries-free permanent teeth. An increasing interest in the dental health needs of the elderly is rapidly developing across Canada with one province having legislation mandating certain basic dental services for the elderly living in institutions. This year saw further development of a program to meet some of the dental needs of elderly residents of government nursing homes. The Children’s Dental Care Program has as its objective, the achievement and maintenance of good dental health by all children in the province. The focus of the program is health promotion and the prevention of dental disease, combined with early, regular dental treat- ment where required. The program provides dental health education, preventive services and dental treatment. Services are delivered in mobile and permanent Department of Health & Social Services Clinics and in private dental offices in a total of seventeen centres throughout the province. Extensive case finding and follow-up procedures are utilized to ensure that all eligible pre- school and school-aged children
permanent Department of Health & Social Services Clinics and in private dental offices in a total of seventeen centres throughout the province. Extensive case finding and follow-up procedures are utilized to ensure that all eligible pre- school and school-aged children receive regular care beginning at an early age. Dental Health Education is provided to parents and children in all clinics. Dental hygienists give presentations in kindergartens and to youth and other groups. During the year division staff visited day care centres and elementary schools in the province and participated in a variety of health promotional activities. Preventive Dental Services are provided in all mobile and fixed dental clinics and in preven- tive clinics which operate throughout the province. Preventive services include cleaning of teeth, the topical application of fluoride and placement of fissure sealants. In 1989-90 a total of 18,129 children received preventive services at seventeen centres. Dental treatment is provided in Department clinics and by private dentists in various centres throughout the province. During 1989-90 a total of 20,510 children received dental treatment. Of this number, 13,540 were treated by private dentists while 6,970 were treated in Department of Health and Social Services’ Clinics. Progress Toward Objective In 1971, when the program commenced, the dental health of children in the province was deplorable. The average child had two infected teeth with seven additional teeth requiring large restorations (fillings). Regular dental care was being received by only 20 percent of school-aged children and 5 percent of pre-school children.

There are currently 18 long- term care facilities in the province, nine public manors and nine licensed private nursing homes, with a total of 968 beds, including respite and temporary beds. Nursing home admission is for individuals who require 24 hour registered nurse (nursing care) supervision and care management. The standardized Seniors Assessment Screening Chapter 3 — Prince Edward Island Tool is used to determine service needs of residents for all admissions to nursing homes. Significant changes were made to long-term nursing care funding and subsidization in Janurary, 2007. First, self-paying residents in nursing homes are no longer required to cover the health care portion of their cost and are only required to cover their accommodation cost. Secondly, eligibility for subsi- dization was changed to be based on an assessment of income rather than on the applicant's total finan- cial resources which previously included income and assets. pages.text: INTRODUCTION In 1988, 67 Manitoba Communities, representing 756,000 people were receiving artificially fluoridated drinking water from 50 water treatment plants. In addition, one Provincial and two Federal waterworks facilities practiced artificial fluoridation. All of the above 50 water treatment plants participated in Manitoba Health's Fluoridation Monitoring Program. This report consists of a summary of how the Fluoridation Program performed, a brief description of improvements and problem areas along with an example of the tabulated results from the Sampling Program and covering letters which were sent to the individual water plant owners. In a few cases, a suggestion was made in the covering letters regarding how the operation of the fluoridation equipment could be improved. Three water treatment plants serving approximately three thousand residents successfully installed and began operating fluoridation equipment with the assistance of Manitoba Dental Health in 1988. In addition, one Federally operated plant serving a Reserve, which has been fluoridating for a number of years asked to participate in the Fluoride Monitoring Program. Thirty-seven of the 50 treatment plants were visited/inspected at least once in 1988. All community administrative staff, water plant operators, as well as the Chief Public Health Engineer, Water Services Board staff and W.M. Ward staff were co-operative and helpful.

Occupational Fatalities: Alberta, 1993 to 1998 An occupational fatality is the death of a worker which results from a work-related incident or exposure. Alberta Human Resources and Employment classifies occupational fatalities into three general event types: motor vehicle incidents; workplace incident; and occupational disease. Each of these three is described in more details below. Motor Vehicle Incident Motor vehicle incidents typically involve highway vehicles operating on public roads in which the fatally injured worker was either a driver or passenger. This category includes fatalities involving air plane crashes, train crashes, helicopter crashes, and so on. ‘ Fatal workplace incidents consist of cases in which the worker dies at a work site, or dies as a result of injuries sustained at a work site. It is this type of occupational fatality that Alberta Human Resources and Employment may be responsible for investigating. Occupational Disease Occupational disease fatalities consist mostly of recognized occupational disease, that is, disease known to be primarily or exclusively work-related (eg., asbestosis, black lung disease). Occupational disease are frequently diagnosed many years after the initial or crucial exposure to the toxic substance, and in such cases it is very difficult to determine when the fatal exposure occurred. The occupational disease category, then, should not be interpreted to reflect present work site hazardous conditions or exposures. Each year the WCB accepts some occupational fatality claims for compensation. The table below shows the number of fatality claims accepted by the type of event. Profile of the Dental Health Plan The Dental Health Plan comprises a children’s dental component and a social assistance component. The children’s dental program covers the following basic dental services for all children, up to and including age twelve: . examinations (at six month intervals) ° cleanings (at 12 month intervals) ° fluoride applications (ages six to 12 at 12 month intervals), except in areas where the School Rinse Program is in place ° x-rays (with some limitations) . fillings and extractions ° other specific procedures which require approval before treatment These basic services are also available under the social assistance component to recipients of social assistance who are 13 to 17 years of age. Adult recipients of social assistance are eligible for emergency care and extractions only. In the changing environment of medical treatment, there are specific occasions where dental procedures are essential to the success of medical procedures (e.g., cancer treatment, organ transplants, and drug therapies). In selective instances of severely compromised medical treatment, the Dental Health Plan may be required to provide necessary dental procedures. Coverage in these instances will be determined on a case by case basis. Each beneficiary covered by the Dental Health Plan must pay a variable amount directly to the dentist for each service provided (e.g. fillings, extractions, etc.). Where a beneficiary is in receipt of social assistance, this co-payment fee is paid by the Dental Health Plan under the social assistance component. pages.text: INTRODUCTION Basic Health Services were provided to the residents of Alberta during the Plan Year July Ist, 1969 to June 30th, 1970 in accordance with the terms of The Alberta Health Care Insurance Act and The Health Insurance Premiums Act and the federal Medical Care Act. The Alberta Legislation reflects the four basic requirements of the Medical Care Act. 1. Coverage of at least 90% of residents of Province. 2. Operation of the Plan by a Provincial Authority. 3. Provision of Insured Services upon Uniform Terms and Conditions to all Residents. 4. Portability of Insured Services between Provinces operating under the Medical Care Act. With the increase of the College of Physicians and Surgeons’ sug- gested Schedule of Fees effective July Ist, 1969, the Commission’s Schedule of Benefits was at the level of 93.5% of the College’s Schedule. Physicians were not required to ‘ SEES ‘opt in’’ or ‘‘opt out’ of the Plan and had the privilege of charg- ing patients an additional amount for their services, providing they made an arrangement or agreement with the patient before the service was _ provided. In addition to the insured services demanded under the federal Medical Care Act, the Plan provides the following for limited coverage of services: Optometry, Chiropractic, Podiatry and Osteopathy. RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE COMMISSION The Commission is the Public Authority responsible under the Acts and regulations for the administration and operation of the Plan. The Commission makes by-laws prescribing the rates of benefits to be paid for practitioners’ services and may enter into arrangements or make agreements for the payment to practitioners on other than a fee-for-service basis.

pages.text: 16. The Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act, and more particularly the regulations under this Act, provide for common or generic names of products being displayed on the label. Regulation 14 (b) states: "The following information shall be shown on the principal display panel:...the identity of the prepackaged product in terms of its common or generic name or in terms of its function." We have here the essence of one of the key terms of the OSHA Proposed Draft Standard, although an alternative to the common or generic name is provided, viz., identification of the product "in terms of its function." The Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act, how- ever, is not intended to provide protection to workers, but only to consumers. This is made clear in Regulation 3(1): "Prepackaged products that are produced or manufactured for commercial or industrial enterprises or institutions for use by such enterprises or institutions without being sold by them as prepackaged products to other consumers are exempt from all the provisions of the Act." Thus if we wish to find Canadian law which protects the citizen as worker to the same extent as the citizen as consumer is protected, . shall have to look elsewhere for it. The Hazardous Products Act, as itsname applies, is intended to apply to known hazardous products only. Moreover, being administered by Consumer and Corporate Affairs, it is intended to protect the consumer and not the worker. A brief overview of this Act reveals some interesting character- istics. In this Act, a “hazardous product" is one which is included on one of two lists. Products on the first list, Part I of the Schedule, are dis- allowed. These include such products as jequirity beans; children's furniture finished with lead paint; toys containing carbon tetrachloride, methyl alcohol, petroleum distillates, benzene, etc.

pages.text: 44 Reaching Outward benefits would flow primarily from the drop in consumer prices and from the associated increases in personal income caused by falling trade barriers. Because con- sumers live in all parts of the country, the gains from such a deal would be very widely dispersed. And while a greater proportion of the job losses would occur in the manufacturing sector, our research indicates that the losses would be transitional and not permanent. Overall, the job gains would outnumber job losses by a ratio of three to one. pages.text: 90 quality of life for the thousands of health-care workers in the hospital workplace. In Metropolitan Toronto, for example, only two hospitals support a full-time occupational medical director: Wellesley Hospital/Princess Margaret Hospital, and The Toronto Hospital/Toronto General and Western Divisions. In addition to the lay assumption that hospitals are inherently healthful places in which to work, there are other factors that have inhibited the development of health and safety programs. The ‘treatment-of- disease’ orientation has tended to pre-—empt competing interests in preventive medicine and health maintenance, while preoccupation with the patient’s care and environment took precedence over the people providing such care. Professional and technological staff were assumed to be self- sufficient in the management of their own oc- cupational health, while support staff often had little guidance at all. The availability of spontaneous informal medical opinion and/or treatment often aborted the reporting process of work-related health concerns and hindered the need for a more or- ganized response. Finally, hospital funding, whether from government, direct patient accounts or en—- dowments, has always been committed to direct patient care along with the other twin priorities of teaching and research. Only during the last decade have funds been more willingly allocated to employee occupational health and the monitoring of environmental biohazards. In Ontario, hospital unions formerly pursued monetary and benefit considerations. However, the occupational health and safety legislation has established a link between hospitals and the Ministry of Labour, and has caused unions to focus on occupational health issues in hospitals. One of the difficulties in addressing occupational health in hospitals is the diversity of the work done —the multiple services, both clinical and support, collectively reflecting a complex organization that never rests and whose demands span a huge range of human capability. Until recently, there was relatively little pedestrian or motor traffic across the Harbourfront/ Railway Lands boundary but, with intensive development of the two sites, and the construc- tion of SkyDome, circumstances have changed dramatically. The Gardiner/Lakeshore transportation corridor, once located on an isolated stretch of an industrialized port, is today part of an increasingly dense urban area. Therefore, it is crucially important that every possible oppor- tunity be taken to provide a large number of crossings for pedestrians moving to and from the waterfront. It is equally vital that redevelopment proposals on both sides of the cor- ridor meet the need for pedestrian and vehicular crossings, and be sensitive in terms of site planning and organization to preserve sight lines and enhance the sense of approach to the water. At present, the tendency of both Harbourfront and the Railway Lands is to turn away from their admittedly difficult common boundary. Clearly, if workable links to the waterfront are to be forged, the time has come for the responsible corpo- rations and groups to abandon the traditional preference for treating Harbourfront and the Railway Lands as if they were two solitudes. Doing that will mean that a number of develop- ment groups, as well as the City of Toronto and Metro Toronto, must be willing to work co-operatively to achieve common goals and the common good. arrive souvent que les premiers symptémes de la maladie ne soient pas correctement identifiés car ils sont communs a d'autres affections. Sans traitement, la blastomycose peut devenir une maladie grave. Tout dépendant des symptémes, un échantillon des mucosités, de pus, d’'urine ou des lésions cutanées pourrait permettre d’établir un diagnostic. Une fois la maladie diagnostiquée, le traitement doit étre prompt et il risque de s’étaler sur plusieurs mois. Comment éviter la blastomycose? Méme si vous devez travailler, vivre ou voyager dans un lieu favorable a la reproduction du champignon, rappelez-vous bien que la blastomycose est une maladie rare et que la probabilité de l'attraper est trés faible. Il est trés difficile de détecter la présence du champignon dans un échantillon de sol et les résultats sont peu fiables. Lexposition au champignon rentraine pas automatiquement l'infection. De ce fait, il n'est pas nécessaire que les gens évitent tout particuligrement un endroit donné. On posséde peu d'information sur les endroits ott, pour un temps donné, pousse le champignon, ni sur Northwestern Health Unit les conditions qui en favorisent ou en empéchent le développement dans le sol. Si votre systeme immunitaire est affaibli, vous voudrez peut-étre éviter toute activité nécessitant un contact avec la terre. Il n'y a pas de vaccin contre la blastomycose. Sans donner de garantie, lorsque vous travaillez dans des endroits humides propices au développement du champignon (sous la maison, le chalet, la galerie ou la remise, par exemple), certaines précautions, comme porter des gants de travail, des souliers appropriés, des pantalons longs, une chemise a manches longues et un masque filtre & poussiére HEPA N100 jetable approuvé par le NIOSH pourraient vous permettre de prévenir la blastomycose. pages.text: Préface En réponse a la préoccupation croissante du public quant aux effets possibles des sites contaminés sur l'environnement et la santé des humains le Conseil canadien des ministres de l'Environnement (CCME) a mis sur pied le Programme national d’assainissement des lieux contaminés (PNALC) en vue de |'évaluation et de la décontamination des lieux contaminés au Canada. Pour favoriser l'uniformité dans I’évaluation des lieux en vertu du Programme, le CCME a demandé que soit mis au point un systéme national de classification des lieux contaminés. Le Systéme national de classification des lieux contaminés est un outil de sélection destiné a faciliter "'évaluation des lieux contaminés en fonction des répercussions néfastes actuelles ou potentielles sur la santé des humains et I'environnement. Il a été élaboré @ la suite d'un examen et d'une évaluation détaillés des méthodes provinciales, territoriales et internationales de classification des lieux contaminés et apres un relevé des types de renseignements mis a la disposition des gestionnaires des lieux contaminés au Canada. La présente version du Systéme national de classification a également fait l'objet de nombreux essais en situation réelle. On a également préparé le systeme sous forme de base de données informatisée dans le but de faciliter le stockage, le rappel et la mise a jour efficaces des données de classification relatives aux lieux con- taminés.

pages.text:
Juvenile Justice The Juvenile Justice Branch provides, or supports the development of, services and resources in Yukon communities to facilitate the rehabilitation of young offenders. Its objective is to do this in a manner that encourages community involvement with, and responsibility for, young offenders and youth crime prevention. Services to young offenders include: * pre-court services, including crime prevention activities and development of community-based alternatives to the court process; ¢ pre-dispositional services, i.e. preparation of reports and assessments for use by the court before a youth is sentenced; e post-dispositional services, i.e. supervision of youth on community-based sentences for probation, community work, treatment groups, and/or counselling; ¢ custody services, with detention and open custody provided in group homes in Whitehorse and secure custody contracted through the province of British Columbia. Significant branch activities in 1987/88 included the development and passage of the Young Persons Offences Act, which substan- tially improves the handling of offences under territorial or municipal statutes. Negotiations underway since 1984 culminated in the signing of a Canada-Yukon cost-sharing agreement, under which the federal government will provide 50% of juvenile justice services funding. In addition, a feasibility study for the implementation of ar automated, record- keeping and statistical information system on young offenders was completed. The number of young offenders served during 1987/88 was 288, a 24% increase over the previous year, with 96% of that growth occurring in Whitehorse. For the second year in a row, the proportion of female young offenders to males showed an increase. pages.text: Chapter 4 Discussion 4.1 Limitations of the study: 4.1.1 Scope This review did not address all the aspects of patients occupying an acute care bed when they could have been cared for more appropriately in another setting. This study looked at the barriers to transition - what delays or barriers prevented timely discharge from acute care? Other issues such as inappropriate admission were not specifically considered. In planning this review, the Team was aware that utilization management reporting in a format that allowed comparison was non-existent in the province. There was no one standardized tool in use that all hospital administrators, physicians, nurses or discharge planners were familiar with and using on a regular basis. Therefore, it is acknowledged that the results are affected by a learning curve. It has been shown that when institutions first employ utilization management techniques and tools, there tends to be under reporting at first while the participants learn to recognize the nuances of the new system. Many of the participants in this study were not familiar with utilization review tools and techniques. 4.1.2 Use of a new survey instrument In order to have a consistent reporting tool for use province-wide, the Team developed a new survey instrument. Although care was taken to have input from the stakeholders and to have a short pilot test completed prior to dissemination throughout the system, it is recognized that this tool has not been through as rigorous testing as the commercially developed Utilization Management Tools available on the market. To employ such tools would have been extremely time consuming and resource intensive. Facilities Review Survey 31

Prince Edward Island Eighth, Members of the Legislative Assembly will freeze their salaries for a third year — and take a leadership position in terms of fiscal restraint. Other major expenditure measures include the following: During our first mandate, grants and contributions increased by $156 Million, or a growth rate of 6.7 per cent a year. As a general principle, we looked to reduce grants and contributions in the range of three to five per cent — but at the same time, we were mindful of the varying capacity and diverse roles of our community partners. Individual departments carefully reviewed their programs, and collectively identified $11.4 Million in savings, including a $1.1 Million reduction in grants to municipalities, and a 3 per cent reduction in core operating grants to our post-secondary institutions and many non-governmental organizations. We recognize the pressures that this will place on our partners, but we believe that all must share in the task of restoring the fiscal health of the Province. As well, we note that the adjusted grant and contribution base remains significantly above the levels we found when we came to Office in 2007. Second, while the demographics of an aging population play a key role in driving health care costs sharply higher, the reverse holds for our public education system — which has experienced declines in student population over the past number of years. Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's National Centre for Diagnostic Virology Promoting Animal Health Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's Animal and Plant Health Directorate ( Food Protection and Inspection Branch) plays a key role in the continuing fight to protect Canada's livestock population from a host of animal dis- eases. This vitally important yet little-known struggle has been waged by Canadian animal health officials since before Confederation. Today, Canada's livestock pop- ulations are free from most of the serious animal diseases found in many countries of the world thanks, in part, to these efforts. Along with protecting livestock from the suffering caused by such diseases, prevention and control of disease ouK breaks is of vital importance to the economic health of Canada's agricultural sector. International customers must be assured that Canadian livestock and livestock products are disease-free. This is the job of the National Centre for Diagnostic Virology that will be relocated at the Federal Laboratories in Winnipeg. Major functions of the Centre include testing samples from animals to be imported into, or exported from, Canada. Diagnosis of a wide variety of livestock dis- eases caused by viruses constitutes the bulk of testing done at the laboratory. At the forefront of animal disease control is the Centre's Foreign Animal Disease Unit, focussing on diagnostic testing to identify more than 27 foreign viral diseases that could threaten Canadian livestock. Failure to maintain constant vigilance against such diseases could have catastrophic consequences. For example, an outbreak of foot and mouth disease, the world's most feared livestock affliction, could quickly lead to severe international trade embargoes by countries free from the disease. Will vaccination eradicate brucellosis? No. Vaccination plays a useful role in controlling the spread of the disease. In the early stages of brucel- losis control in Canada, vaccination reduced the level of infection to a point where it was possible to proceed with a test-and-slaughter program to eradicate the disease and establish areas free from brucellosis. As we are now reaching the final stages of brucellosis eradication, there is less need for a vaccination program. Should an owner continue a vaccination program in his herd? The Health of Animals Branch considers that it is no longer necessary to carry out a vaccination program except where the incidence of brucellosis in a herd or an area warrants it. What safeguards are taken to ensure that an area remains free of brucellosis infection? The Health of Animals Branch conducts two screen- ing programs: Brucellosis Milk Ring Tests — Milk and cream sam- ples collected at dairies and creameries are tested for brucellosis. Market Cattle Testing — Cattle are identified with special back tags and are blood-tested at markets and slaughtering plants. If infection is uncovered by either of the above screening programs, the entire herd is blood-tested and the source of infection is thoroughly investigated. Herds not covered by one of these plans are periodically blood-tested for brucellosis. The above tests provide adequate assurance that sources of infection introduced into a herd will be uncovered early, thus preventing the infection from spreading within the herd or to other herds. Will heifers and cows that are not vaccinated be eligible for export? Yes. The Common Market countries of Europe have discontinued vaccination and are requesting non- vaccinated animals. The United States Department of Agriculture is de- emphasizing vaccination. Many States now require that an animal be negative to a brucellosis test when 18
The Common Market countries of Europe have discontinued vaccination and are requesting non- vaccinated animals. The United States Department of Agriculture is de- emphasizing vaccination. Many States now require that an animal be negative to a brucellosis test when 18 months of age or over. In many cases, this is a difficult requirement to meet in a vaccinated animal.

Like the previous non-water using systems, the use of composting toilets to manage human waste within the home environ- ment represents a complete break with conventional plumbing. The pro- totype of a composting system was first installed in a home in 1939 by its Swedish inventor, Carl Lindstrom, but is a relatively new concept in the technology of waste disposal in North America (Stoner, 1977). Units based on early designs use a large, well ventilated container located in the basement of buildings, and receive wastes through verticle chutes connected to the toilet and kitchen. The container is vented through the roof of the building. The container has three sloping sections: the excrement chamber; the refuse chamber; and the storage chamber. Decomposition generates heat which induces natural convection and draws air through and over the compost heap, keeping it nearly aerobic and carrying away evaporated moisture. As the organic material decomposes, it falls slowly down the inclined, ventilated slope, which is the key to the process, to the storage chamber where it remains until manually removed. pages.text: DESCRIPTION By its promotion of physical activity through financial contributions and consultative services, Fitness Canada works to develop fitness leadership nation-wide and to encourage participation in physical activity leading toward fitness of all Canadians. In addition, it has identified specific target groups for special emphasis. Major activities are grouped under four areas of fitness development: Promotion, Education, Leadership Development and Research. Promotion Fitness Canada has undertaken a major commitment to the national promotion of fitness as evidenced by the formation of PARTICIPaction in 1971. With ongoing financial support from Fitness Canada ($1,016,000 in 1985/86 to date) the PARTICIPaction promotional campaign works to increase Canadians' awareness of the benefits of fitness and encourages them to aim for higher rates of participation in physical activity. Fitness Canada also supports opportunities for general participation in physical activity. On this basis, financial assistance has been provided for a number of participation development projects run by national associations. In addition, Fitness Canada has developed and currently operates National Physical Activity Week in cooperation with a number of national Organizations and provincial governments. This major initiative strives to raise the general awareness of the benefits of physical activity. The Canada Fitness Award serves as an incentive for Canadian youth by promoting increased standards of achievement and thereby encouraging regular physical activity leading toward fitness. Education Fitness Canada has also initiated and supported a number of educational activities which are designed to upgrade the knowledge of both the consumer and those individuals involved in the development of physical activity and fitness programs. Physical education in schools confers psycho-social benefits to children and youth in addition to the obvious physical benefits.°° A recent meta-analysis by Ekeland and colleagues suggests that exercise has positive short-term effects on self-esteem in children and young people.°*° Other research demonstrates that active adolescents are significantly less likely to initiate risky behaviours such as smoking and drug use and are significantly more likely to express confidence in their health.° d. Enhanced Academic Performance Strong academic performance is the central outcome all schools strive for. School health and physical education help to foster this outcome by indirectly supporting academic achievement. In fact, data collected over the course of the past two decades indicate that health and physical education programs and initiatives exert positive influences on academic performance in children and youth.*°”°*°9 Mathematics and reading scores are common measures used to assess the impact of health education and comprehensive school health initiatives on academic performance. Work by Schoener, Guerrero, and Whitney (1988) found that reading and mathematics scores of third and fourth grade students who received comprehensive health education were significantly higher than those who did not receive this kind of in-school programming.” The effect of health education on academic performance is especially profound for at-risk youth. Comprehensive health education and social skills programs for this population of students has been shown to improve overall academic and test performance.©’ Moreover, this benefit has been shown to be sustainable over time based on longitudinal studies.™ Physical education and physical activity initiatives, independent of any other health, nutrition or wellness curricula, has been linked to benefits that extend to academic performance. Data from randomized, controlled trials are lacking. However, correlational studies document relationships between physical activity and enhanced academic performance.®' For example, a 2001 study of almost 8000 children between the ages of
linked to benefits that extend to academic performance. Data from randomized, controlled trials are lacking. However, correlational studies document relationships between physical activity and enhanced academic performance.®' For example, a 2001 study of almost 8000 children between the ages of 7 and 15 years observed significant positive correlations between self- reported physical activity and results of standardized fitness tests with academic performance.®' Similarly, results from the California Physical Fitness Test (2002) reveal strong positive relationships between physical fitness and academic achievement.” The evidence counters the notion that physical education curricula or physical activity initiatives detract from academic pursuits. A systematic review of coordinated or comprehensive school health programs by Murray et al (2007) found that strong evidence exists for a lack of negative effects of physical education programs on academic outcomes.®’ Evidence dating back to the late 1970s shows that physical education supports rather than detracts from academic success.®° For example, a randomized trial of physical education programs incorporating fitness or skill training for 75 minutes per day, compared to the programs offered for 30 minutes three times per week demonstrated no significant decrement in test scores compared to controls.” This work suggests that implementation of a rigorous physical education curriculum does not impair academic achievement on standardized tests. 12 / A Review and Synthesis of Related Literature Wellness Curricula 2008 ©Alberta Education, Alberta, Canada

These pages cover only some places and groups, not the whole country.

Un rapport communautaire de 1997-1998 dit que certaines personnes voyaient la « vie active » comme une idée positive. Ces pages ne couvrent que certains lieux et groupes, pas tout le pays.

answer.en: Pages from 1985 to 2002 mention physical fitness. A 1985 page says physical education is compulsory in the schools until grade 9. A 2002 list of teacher resources describes a guide to using large exercise balls to help children develop coordination, balance, rhythm and fitness skills. These pages do not give one overall view of fitness for all of Canada.

Une liste de ressources pédagogiques de 2002 décrit un guide sur l'usage de gros ballons d'exercice pour aider les enfants à développer la coordination, l'équilibre, le rythme et la condition physique. Ces pages ne donnent pas une vue d'ensemble pour tout le Canada.

answer.en: By 2008 the pages talk about physical fitness mostly in schools. A 1985 page describes a school course that emphasizes physical fitness. A 2008 Alberta review of wellness curricula cites results from the California Physical Fitness Test (2002) that show strong positive links between physical fitness and academic achievement. The pages do not give a full picture of fitness across the country.
answer.fr: En 2008, les pages parlent surtout de condition physique à l'école. Une page de 1985 décrit un cours scolaire axé sur la condition physique. Une revue albertaine de 2008 sur les programmes de mieux-être cite des résultats d'un test de condition physique de la Californie (2002) qui montrent des liens positifs forts entre la condition physique et la réussite scolaire. Les pages ne donnent pas un portrait complet pour tout le pays.

answer.en: The pages talk about fitness in schools and in government programs. A 1985 page says a course that emphasizes physical fitness must be taken in grade 10, 11 or 12. A 2008 Alberta review cites California test results linking physical fitness with academic achievement. A 2010 Nova Scotia page advises combining three types of physical activity for best results. The pages do not give a single overall view of fitness.

answer.en: The pages say different things about fitness over the years. A 1985 page describes a school course that emphasizes physical fitness, and a 2008 Alberta review cites California test results linking fitness with academic achievement. A 2015 Saskatchewan audit says one school division tested Grade 9 and 10 students' fitness. The pages do not give a full picture of fitness across Canada.

adjudication.reason: Every quote is on its page, but four epoch answers overreached. The 2008, 2010 and 2015 answers said a 2008 Alberta review found fitness linked to school marks; the page cites California Physical Fitness Test results, so they now say that. The 1990, 1998 and 2002 answers called the 1985 page New Brunswick, which neither the page nor its metadata says, and the 2002 answer described a 'fitness image of the 1970s and 1980s' that is not in the quote; both removed. Rewritten in both languages from the quotes only.

claude-haiku-5-5.notes: The round's answer for 1963 says the pages say nothing about fitness, which is fair, but the epoch answers and explanation overreach: 1990 and 2010 answers cite a New Brunswick grade-10-to-12 course and Alberta/Nova Scotia pages not matching the year framing; 1985 answer says a course covers fitness while the page says the course emphasizes fitness, and the 1998 text describes the Active Living concept accurately but 'Physical education compulsory until grade 9' is attributed to a 1985 New Brunswick page that is fine. Key problem: the 2008 answer says fitness results show positive links with school marks from a 2008 Alberta review, but that concerns California fitness tests, not Alberta school marks; 2015 answer says one division tested Grade 9 and 10 students, which is supported. Quotes include a Sports Medicine item and mislabelled 'y' quote IDs. The dial answers mix years and overstate what pages establish, and the 1963 and 1976 states are 'insufficient' while quotes list items; the round is confusing for visitors and needs a human check before display.

gpt-oss-120b.notes: All epoch answers are consistent with the evidence provided; the statements about the presence or absence of fitness-related information are supported by the quoted pages, and the language is clear and appropriate for visitors.

verdicts.notes: All quotes match their pages verbatim and each epoch summary (hospital lists with Physiotherapy/Physical Medicine, NB rehabilitation committee, 1977 sports medicine clinic, girls' activity after 15, Fitness Canada's four areas, Active Living in The Pas, Swiss-ball teacher resource, fitness-academic links, Grade 9-10 fitness testing) is traceable to the cited pages. French tracks the English closely; the 1990 French drops 'leading toward fitness' and uses 'Fitness Canada' where earlier epochs say 'Condition physique Canada', both minor.

Even though fluoride-containing food, water and other beverages are ingested, what is of importance is the ultimate amount of fluoride absorbed by the body. Studies by others indicate that the site of fluoride absorption in humans is the entire gastro-intestinal tract (WHO, 1970). Fluorides ingested in foods are not as completely assimilated as are fluorides in water. Over 85% of the fluoride in water is absorbed, whereas only about one third to one half of fluoride in foods is assimilated (Nikiforuk, 1985). Continuous ingestion of above optimum amounts of fluoride can produce a condition known as dental fluorosis. This condition appears as mottling of the tooth enamel. It can range from very mild, with a few opaque white areas, to severe cases in which entire teeth are pitted and/or stained brown. This condition was first noticed in communities with very high natural concentra- tions of fluorides in their drinking water. 28

pages.text: IV. MONITORING PROGRAM A. OVERVIEW The purpose of this program is to ensure that the recommended level for fluoride concentration is maintained in Manitoba's drinking water. All sixty-six (66) water treatment plants participated. 1) Manitoba Health identifies an operating range and an optimum level for fluoride concentration in drinking water. The optimum is | part per million (p.p.m.) or | milligram per litre (mg/l). The operating range for 1999 / 2000 was set at 0.80 p.p.m. as a minimum with 1.20 p.p.m. as a maximum. Water treatment plant operators are encouraged to maintain fluoride concentrations within the specified range. Manitoba Health provides a schedule for bi-weekly monitoring periods. A sampling year consists of 26 periods. Manitoba Health provides Fluoridation Control Record forms to the plants, to be submitted with the samples. Manitoba Health also provides sampling bottles, fluoride standard solution, spadns (reagent) and shipping containers to the plants, through the EnviroTest Laboratories. All are necessary for daily testing and bi-weekly sample submission. Samples are collected on a daily basis, tested on-site and results are recorded by the water treatment plant operator. A 14 day composite sample (approximately one litre) is submitted bi-weekly by the community for analysis. A record of chemical feed data (Fluoridation Control Record) is submitted with the sample. The EnviroTest Laboratories located in Winnipeg, receives the samples and conducts the analysis. The results are reported to the individual water treatment plant operators and to Manitoba Health. Manitoba Health monitors the levels, makes recommendations, and provides technical assistance accordingly. Communities receive an annual report of their plant's operating record. On a periodic and/or as required basis, reports are provided during the operating year.

OFFICE OF THE OmBUDSMAN —— lessees One of the concerns we heard from the public during this investigation was that there is a lack of publicly available information about drinking water.'”° The following response to the drinking water questionnaire that we posted on our website illustrates this point: Most water quality data collected on public water supply systems is not very comprehensive and not made public. For example, why can't I go to a website and find data on every registered public water supply system in BC? | may be researching arsenic or fluoride concentrations in Public water supplies and ready access to this data could be valuable. Or I may be concerned that a pregnant woman is drinking water that may have elevated nitrate concentrations. Why can't | get this information without resorting to a freedom of information request? As this respondent points out, currently there is no single central source of information on drinking water that is accessible to the public that consumes the water and to those supplying it. Instead, information is collected by different groups, in different manners, for different purposes. For example, the Ministry of Environment uses several databases, commonly known as the “legacy systems.” These include the environmental monitoring system (EMS): the water licensing information system (WLIS): the well. aquifer and contact information system (WELLS): and the water inventory data management system (WIDM). As well, each of the regional health authorities has its own database. Some regional health authorities use a database program called HealthSpace for this purpose, while the others use a program called HedgeHog. These databases are used to collect information, including that related to water system facilities, hazard and risks ratings, and water sample testing. Health Canada and Environment Canada have reviewed and assessed inorganic fluorides under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999 (CEPA 1999) (Canada, 1999). The screening assessment concluded that levels of inorganic fluorides normally found in the Canadian environment are not considered harmful to human health but are a concern for the environment (Environment Canada & Health Canada, 1993). Inorganic fluorides are listed on Schedule 1, List of Toxic Substances, under CEPA 1999. The Act allows the federal government to control the importa- tion, manufacture, distribution, and use of inorganic fluorides in Canada (Canada, 1999; Canada, 2000). Health Canada does not consider fluoride to be an essential element and recommends that fluoride requirements be based only on the beneficial effect on dental caries (Health Canada, 2010a). Young children tend to swallow toothpaste during brushing, so guide- lines have been established that strive to balance the health risks with the health benefits of fluoride use. In general, toothpaste use is not recommended for children under the age of 3 and for children 3 to 6 years old, Health Canada recommends supervision during brushing and use of only a small amount of fluoridated toothpaste (Health Canada, 2010b). Health Canada recently completed a review of the health risks associated with fluoride in drinking water in which moderate dental fluorosis was chosen as the endpoint of concern for fluoride (Health Canada, 2010a). Although moderate dental fluorosis is not a health concern and is not considered to be a toxicolog- ical endpoint, Health Canada considers it to be an adverse effect based on its potential aesthetic concern. The current Canadian drinking water quality guideline developed by Health Canada sets out the maximum acceptable concentration of fluoride (Health Canada, 2010a). This guideline is considered to be protective against all potential adverse health effects including those related to cancer,
The current Canadian drinking water quality guideline developed by Health Canada sets out the maximum acceptable concentration of fluoride (Health Canada, 2010a). This guideline is considered to be protective against all potential adverse health effects including those related to cancer, immunotoxic- ity, reproductive/developmental toxicity, genotoxicity, and/or neurotoxicity (Health Canada, 2010a). For communities wishing to fluoridate their water supply, Health Canada has determined an optimal concentra- tion of fluoride in drinking water to promote dental health while protecting against adverse effects (Health Canada, 2010b). Tolerable upper intake levels for fluoride, which account for its potential toxicity, have been developed by the Institute of Medicine and adopted by Health Canada (Health Canada, 2010c; IOM, 1997). The concentration of fluoride in some foods and pre- packaged water and ice is regulated by Health Canada under the Food and Drug Regulations (Canada, 2012). Food tolerances for fluoride currently exist for edible bone meal and fish protein as well as prepackaged ice or water, including those represented as mineral or spring water (Canada, 2012). The first cycle (2007—2009) of the Canadian Health Measures Survey (CHMS) included a National Oral Health Component supported by Health Canada (Health Canada, 2010d). In addition to many other dental considerations, dental fluorosis was measured in children ranging from 6 to 12 years old. The results from cycle 1 of the CHMS found that 60% of chil- dren had teeth considered normal, 24% had enamel with white flecks or spots where the cause was ques- tionable, 12% had one or more teeth with fluorosis classified as very mild, and 4% had fluorosis classified as mild. The prevalence of moderate or severe fluorosis was too low to allow reporting (less than 0.3%). Recent changes As new agencies adopt the Drinking Water Advisories application, they may add retrospective data to the system; results for 2010 to 2015 have been revised accordingly. In this update, the reason "Exceedance of maximum allowable concentrations or drinking water standard” was removed as a reason for issuing a boil water advisory. Although used infrequently, this reason was found to be too generic and its use too variable, as it included both equipment and process-related issues and issues such as turbidity, detection of total coliforms or E. coli. In the current iteration of the indicators, experts have reviewed each individual boil water advisory record citing the reason “Exceedance of maximum allowable concentrations or drinking water standard” in order to find the actual cause of the advisory and to place it in the right category. The advisories previously attributed to this reason are now placed in their respective categories. The data for previous years have been revised accordingly. Therefore, this update may show slightly different data from the previous update. Caveats and limitations The Canadian Network for Public Health Intelligence Drinking Water Advisories application is a national tool developed and enhanced over time through partnerships and collaborative work involving federal, provincial and territorial partners. The front-line users of the system are the regulatory and health protection agencies who oversee drinking water safety. The data in the system belong to these agencies, as they created that data in the course of their oversight activities. The Drinking Water Advisories application became a live surveillance and alerting tool in 2008. The number of agencies using the system is growing each year, and the end goal for the Drinking water advisories indicators is to represent the full national picture. Although this has not yet been achieved, the data are representative of prevailing trends in
agencies using the system is growing each year, and the end goal for the Drinking water advisories indicators is to represent the full national picture. Although this has not yet been achieved, the data are representative of prevailing trends in a variety of regions across Canada and provide useful insight into issues that challenge the delivery of safe drinking water. The Drinking water advisories indicators present an overall view of the trends emerging in the system, rather than focusing on the specific data for any particular province, territory or agency. Percentages reported in these indicators may differ from previous and future publications as historic data are added to the system and as new agencies adopt the application. answer.en: These pages do not say anything about fluoride in drinking water. One 1979 page says some people choose bottled water because they do not like the "chemical additives of municipal water", but it does not name fluoride. The other pages are about hospital supplies and a kitchen index.
answer.fr: Ces pages ne disent rien du fluor dans l'eau potable. Une page de 1979 indique que certaines personnes choisissent l'eau embouteillée parce qu'elles n'aiment pas les « chemical additives of municipal water », mais elle ne nomme pas le fluor. Les autres pages portent sur le matériel d'un hôpital et sur un index de cuisine.

answer.en: Only one page, from the City of Toronto's Department of Public Health in 1983, speaks about fluoride in drinking water. It says the draft guidelines call for a fluoride program where the water has less than 0.7 ppm, and it notes recent trouble keeping fluoride levels up in Metropolitan Toronto. It suggests a supplementary program if fluoride is missing for more than 90 days. The other pages do not cover fluoride, so this is not a full picture.
answer.fr: Une seule page, celle du Service de santé publique de la Ville de Toronto en 1983, parle du fluor dans l'eau potable. Elle dit que l'ébauche de lignes directrices demande un programme de fluor là où l'eau en contient moins de 0,7 ppm, et elle mentionne des difficultés récentes à maintenir les niveaux dans le Toronto métropolitain. Elle propose un programme supplémentaire si l'eau est sans fluor pendant plus de 90 jours. Les autres pages ne traitent pas du fluor, alors ce portrait n'est pas complet.

answer.en: By 1988, two pages speak to fluoride in drinking water. A 1983 Toronto health department response says a fluoride program is required where water has less than 0.7 ppm, and it raises problems keeping fluoride in Toronto's water. A 1988 Northwest Territories report says over 85% of fluoride in water is absorbed, and that too much over time can cause dental fluorosis. The pages do not say whether fluoride in water is right or wrong, or how widely it was used.
answer.fr: En 1988, deux pages parlent du fluorure dans l'eau potable. Une réponse du service de santé de Toronto, en 1983, dit qu'un programme de fluorure est exigé là où l'eau contient moins de 0,7 ppm, et elle signale des difficultés à maintenir le fluorure dans l'eau de Toronto. Un rapport des Territoires du Nord-Ouest de 1988 dit que plus de 85 % du fluorure de l'eau est absorbé, et qu'une trop grande quantité sur une longue période peut causer la fluorose dentaire. Les pages ne disent pas si le fluorure dans l'eau est une bonne ou une mauvaise chose, ni à quel point il était répandu.

answer.en: By 1990, the pages show fluoride in drinking water being discussed in several places. A 1983 Toronto response asked what health units should do if fluoride was missing from the water. A 1988 Northwest Territories report said too much fluoride over time can mottle tooth enamel. A 1990 Manitoba report said about 95% of people on a public water system got fluoridated water. These pages do not cover the rest of Canada.
answer.fr: En 1990, les pages montrent que le fluorure dans l'eau potable est abordé à plusieurs endroits. En 1983, une réponse de Toronto demandait quoi faire si l'eau ne contenait plus de fluorure. Un rapport de 1988 des Territoires du Nord-Ouest disait qu'une trop grande quantité de fluorure, sur une longue période, peut tacheter l'émail des dents. Un rapport manitobain de 1990 disait qu'environ 95 % des gens desservis par un réseau public recevaient de l'eau fluorée. Ces pages ne couvrent pas le reste du Canada.

answer.en: The pages show fluoride being added to drinking water and checked in some places. In Manitoba in 1989, about 95% of people on a public water system received fluoridated water, and by 1999-2000 the province set an operating range of 0.80 to 1.20 p.p.m. A 1988 page says too much fluoride over time can cause tooth mottling. The pages do not cover the rest of Canada in full.
answer.fr: Les pages montrent que du fluorure est ajouté à l'eau potable et vérifié à certains endroits. Au Manitoba, en 1989, environ 95 % des gens desservis par un réseau public recevaient de l'eau fluorée, et en 1999-2000, la province a fixé une plage d'exploitation de 0,80 à 1,20 p.p.m. Une page de 1988 indique qu'un excès de fluorure sur une longue période peut causer des taches sur les dents. Les pages ne couvrent pas tout le reste du Canada.

answer.en: By 2008, the pages include reports on fluoride in drinking water. A 1990 Manitoba report says about 95% of people served by a public water system there received fluoridated water. A 2000 report says Manitoba Health set an optimum fluoride level of 1 part per million. The pages do not say what happened in other provinces or after 2000.
answer.fr: En 2008, les pages comprennent des rapports sur le fluorure dans l'eau potable. Un rapport manitobain de 1990 indique qu'environ 95 % des personnes desservies par un réseau public d'eau recevaient de l'eau fluorée. Un rapport de 2000 indique que Santé Manitoba a fixé un niveau optimal de fluorure de 1 partie par million. Les pages ne disent pas ce qui s'est passé dans les autres provinces ni après 2000.

answer.en: By 2013 the pages say that a Manitoba program, described in 2000, was meant to keep the recommended fluoride level in the province's drinking water, and that Health Canada set a maximum acceptable concentration of fluoride in drinking water. Health Canada also set an optimal level for communities that wish to fluoridate. The pages do not say how many communities across Canada fluoridate their water.
answer.fr: En 2013, les pages disent qu'un programme manitobain, décrit en 2000, visait à maintenir le niveau recommandé de fluorure dans l'eau potable de la province, et que Santé Canada a fixé une concentration maximale acceptable de fluorure dans l'eau potable. Santé Canada a aussi fixé un niveau optimal pour les collectivités qui veulent fluorer leur eau. Les pages ne disent pas combien de collectivités au Canada fluorent leur eau.

answer.en: By 2018, the pages show fluoride in drinking water in several ways. A 1990 Manitoba report says about 95% of people on a public water system there received fluoridated water. A 2013 Health Canada report says it set an optimal fluoride level for communities that want to fluoridate. The pages do not say how many communities across Canada add fluoride.
answer.fr: En 2018, les pages montrent le fluor dans l'eau potable de plusieurs façons. Un rapport manitobain de 1990 indique qu'environ 95 % des gens desservis par un réseau public d'eau y recevaient de l'eau fluorée. Un rapport de Santé Canada de 2013 indique qu'il a établi une concentration optimale de fluorure pour les collectivités qui souhaitent fluorer leur eau. Les pages ne disent pas combien de collectivités au Canada ajoutent du fluorure.

adjudication.reason: Every epoch traces to its quotes. One overreach: the 2013 answer gave Manitoba's 1 part per million optimum as a 2013 statement, but it comes from the 2000 Manitoba page and the quote does not give the number. Rewritten to say what the quotes say and when.

claude-haiku-5-5.notes: Most epoch sentences match the pages and the quotes are accurate. The 2013 epoch attributes the Manitoba 1 ppm optimum to the pages generally, but that figure comes from the 2000 Manitoba page, not a 2013 page, so the wording slightly overreaches. The time-dial answers are honest for each year, and the French is a faithful translation. Nothing is offensive or misleading.

gpt-oss-120b.notes: The epoch answers are well‑supported by the cited pages, correctly reflect the presence or absence of fluoride information, and are clear and appropriate for visitors.

verdicts.notes: Every epoch's claims trace to the cited pages and all quotes match the page text verbatim (0.7 ppm program, 90-day suggestion, Toronto supply shortage, 85% absorption and fluorosis, Manitoba 95% and 0.80–1.20 ppm range, Health Canada maximum and optimal levels); early epochs honestly report no fluoride content. French matches the English in substance; the only oddity is that pages_by_then lists shrink in later epochs, which does not affect the answers.

However, it has already been discovered in the United States that many industrial chemicals now in use are hazardous, and if correctly identified, would be subject to strict controls. That is, they are actually considered dangerous right now, but are being used under trade names which hide their true nature from both the user and the government regulatory agency. As one writer, commenting on a recent National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) occupational hazards survey, put it: "Of those 45,000 trade name industrial chemical products about which NIOSH had ingredient information 45 percent, almost one-half, contained a chemical that was then regulated by OSHA, that is, was either on the TLV list, or was one of the 16 carcinogens then regulated by OSHA ."'> Thus the danger is that, when the regulation process is tightened up in the United States through a strong chemical labelling standard, and certain products can be used there only under tight controls or not at all, then chemical manufacturers (the multinationals, especially) might be tempted to "dump" stocks of these dangerous substances in countries without adequate labelling legislation, and further, might continue to manufacture dangerous substances (under old or new trade names, but not generic or chemical names) for these markets. pages.text: CANADA LIBRARY OF PARLIAMENT BIBLIOTHEQUE DU PARLEMENT TOBACCO SMOKING ISSUE DEFINITION Since the 1960s, research has continued to document the health hazards of both smoking tobacco and inhaling second-hand smoke. At the same time, the anti-smoking lobby has grown increasingly vocal about the social costs of smoking and of tolerating the habit in public places. These groups are pressuring federal and provincial governments to legislate against tobacco advertising and smoking in the workplace, to declare tobacco a hazardous substance and to assist tobacco farmers to find alternative crops or alternative employment. The tobacco farmers, however, want a national marketing board to help maintain prices and to find new markets in Canada and abroad. Tobacco manufacturers are buying less tobacco from farmers because of declining domestic sales of cigarettes, which they blame mainly on rising government taxes, and increased foreign competition for the export market. Rationalization and diversification have maintained profits for some tobacco manufacturers, but communities dependent on tobacco growing are suffering financially because they cannot sell their crops. Health and Welfare Canada has initiated anti-smoking campaigns aimed at youth and has expressed increased concern about the rising health costs associated with the preventable illnesses that result from tobacco use. While placing voluntary restrictions on tobacco advertising, however, the federal government has continued to subsidize the tobacco farmers.
